idiom_name: abstract class with a skeleton + protected abstract steps and protected hook methods
implementation_notes: TypeScript's class syntax gives the pattern directly: an `abstract class` carries the skeleton, `protected abstract` members are the required steps and `protected` methods with bodies are the hooks - the classes handbook states that abstract members must be implemented by subclasses and that an abstract class cannot be instantiated. Because `abstract` and `protected` are erased at compile time, the guarantee is a type-checker guarantee only; structural typing and abundant function values make the factory-function form (closing over the step callbacks) the everyday realization when the steps need no shared state. Keep the abstract-class form when steps mutate instance state or the class is extended by consumers.
pitfalls: `protected` and `abstract` disappear at runtime: consumers of the compiled JavaScript can call or replace any step, so the compiler is the only thing enforcing the contract.
Structural typing means an object literal with the right shape satisfies an interface; the inheritance-based skeleton is only enforced when the class is really extended.

Steps written as arrow-function class fields are per-instance properties initialised after the constructor body starts, so a step called from the base constructor can still be undefined; use prototype methods for steps.
